messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Figures: People in uniform, Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Carry Weapon: carry weapon, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rafael Moreno is a 70-year-old widowed dentist who came to treatment after years of trying to manage on his own what happened during a terrorist attack. He describes the event haltingly and only in fragments, because when he gets close to it he becomes so flooded that he has to stop speaking. Even in early sessions, he would begin, press his lips together, and lift a hand as if to hold the memory back. He said more than once that he could not really put it into words. What returns to him is not a story with a beginning and end so much as a total sensory experience that feels as if it is happening again: the crack of gunfire, the confusion in the room, the presence of armed men, the bodily certainty that death was near. The most he has been able to convey consistently is that he was in a public place when the attack began, that there were men in uniform amid the chaos, and that the sound of gunshots is what still reaches him first, before any thought does.

In the months after the attack, Rafael did what he had always done in his professional life: he tried to stay controlled, practical, and prepared. He returned to his dental practice, but his days began to narrow around signs of danger. The first thing he noticed on entering any building, including his own office, was where the exits were. He would register them before he noticed the receptionist’s greeting or the patient schedule. In the waiting room he found himself studying people closely, not out of curiosity but from a felt need to judge whether anyone might be dangerous. A patient shifting suddenly in his seat, a stranger lingering near the front desk, a delivery worker in a uniform stepping into the suite could change the whole atmosphere for him in an instant. He would feel his body tighten before he had fully taken in why.

Specific things came to carry a charge that was immediately understandable to him, even if he hated living this way. People in uniform were especially difficult. A police officer walking past the storefront below his office, a security guard in a medical building, even seeing someone dressed in a style that reminded him of military clothing would pull his attention hard. Conversations about the military were almost as bad. If patients or colleagues began talking about deployments, weapons, wars, or “service,” Rafael felt himself leaving the present and bracing internally, as though something threatening were already unfolding around him. Gunshot noises were the most potent of all. Fireworks, a car backfiring, a sharp bang from construction near the office could send him into immediate alarm. He described being on high alert with any loud or unexpected sound, his body reacting before his mind caught up.

Over time, Rafael built his life around reducing contact with anything that might bring the attack too close. He stopped watching news coverage about shootings, bombings, or attacks because even a brief report could leave him shaken for hours. He began carrying a weapon, telling himself that at his age, living alone after his wife’s death, it was only sensible to be able to protect himself. He knew this was not how he had lived before, but the weapon gave him a sense that he was not entirely exposed. Alongside this, another pattern settled in: he repeatedly blamed himself for what had happened. He would replay scraps of the day and circle around the same questions—whether he should have noticed something earlier, moved faster, chosen a different place to stand, done more for other people. These thoughts did not resolve into answers, but he returned to them again and again.

The strain has become visible in the texture of his daily life. At the practice, he schedules fewer patients and dislikes being in the office when there is unfamiliar foot traffic in the hallway. He has become more guarded with staff and more distracted when sudden noises break the routine of the day. Socially he is narrower too, avoiding situations where current events are likely to come up. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent incident at work when a sharp bang from nearby construction made the memory return with such force that he had to stop in the middle of the day and shut himself in his office. He said it was as if the attack had arrived whole, through sound and sensation, and for several minutes he was no longer certain he was in his dental practice. That frightened him not only because of how real it felt, but because he could see how much of his life had come to revolve around staying ready, staying armed, staying watchful. What he hopes for now is modest but deeply felt: to be able to walk into his own office without first planning escape, to hear a loud sound without feeling that he is back there, and to speak about what happened without being overtaken by it.
